source_text: I. Communis Ecclesiae Romanae Doctrina est, primum hominem, antequam Diabolo instigante peccaret, praeditum fuisse vera justitia & sanctitate, cujus respectu Deo gratus & acceptus erat ad vitam aeternam. Id manifeste docet Concilium ipsum Tridentinum Sessione quinta decreto De peccato Originali. Ubi anathema dicit, illi qui non confitetur primum hominem Adam, cum mandatum Dei in paradiso fuisset transgressus, statim sanctitatem & justitiam in qua constitutus fuerat amisisse. Et praeterea illi qui asserit Adamum acceptam a Deo sanctitatem & justitiam quam perdidit, sibi soli, & non nobis etiam perdidisse.
english: The common teaching of the Roman Church is that the first man, before he sinned at the devil's prompting, was endowed with true righteousness and holiness, on account of which he was pleasing and acceptable to God for eternal life.

The Council of Trent itself teaches this plainly in its fifth session, in the decree on original sin. There it pronounces anathema on anyone who does not confess that the first man, Adam, when he had broken God's command in paradise, at once lost the holiness and righteousness in which he had been placed. It pronounces it too on anyone who asserts that the holiness and righteousness Adam received from God and then lost, he lost for himself alone and not for us as well.

source_text: II. Porro justitia & sanctitas illa, ex mente Doctorum Ecclesiae Romanae, non in eo solum consistebat, quod mens hominis imbuta erat vera Dei cognitione, & quae ad aeternae beatitudinis adeptionem sufficeret; ejus vero voluntas puro & casto amore Deum complectebatur: sed praeterea in eo quod caro spiritui, & corpus animae sine difficultate & repugnantia parebat, & appetitus sensitivus ita rationis ductum sequebatur, ut adversus eam nunquam rebellaret, & in diversa hominem traheret: ac proinde Adam in illo integritatis statu nullam in se luctam carnis & spiritus, nullamque membrorum adversus legem mentis rebellionem, qualem frequenter in nobis sentimus, experiretur: sed ad bonum ferretur, & a malo sese averteret sine pugna & difficultate, neque haberet in se praedictam illam concupiscentiam, cum qua jam nascimur, & quae usque ad mortem in nobis perseverat.
english: In the view of the Roman Church's teachers, that righteousness and holiness did not consist only in man's mind being filled with a true knowledge of God, enough for gaining eternal blessedness, and in his will embracing God with pure and chaste love.

It also consisted in this: the flesh obeyed the spirit and the body the soul without difficulty or resistance, and the sensual appetite followed reason's lead so fully that it never rebelled against it or pulled the man in different directions.

So Adam in that unfallen state felt within himself no struggle of flesh against spirit, and no rebellion of his members against the law of his mind, such as we often feel. He moved toward good and turned away from evil without conflict or difficulty, and he did not have in him the concupiscence spoken of above, with which we are now born and which stays with us until death.

source_text: III. Quaeritur autem an ista justitia & sanctitas primo homini fuerit naturalis, necne? Ad quam quaestionem ut respondeant Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, observant naturale variis modis sumi. Primo enim naturale dicitur omne quod habetur a nativitate: & ita naturale opponitur adventitio. Secundo naturale vocatur illud quod est naturae consentaneum, quodque naturam non destruit, sed potius ornat & perficit. Quo sensu naturale opponitur ei quod est contra naturam. Tertio naturale vocatur quod aut est pars naturae, aut fluit ex principiis naturae, vel ab illis fluere aptum est. Qua significatione corpus & animus, facultates quoque tum sentiendi, tum intelligendi, & operationes quae ab eis facultatibus, absque auxilio naturam superante exercentur, naturalia dicuntur: & ita naturale opponitur supernaturali.
english: The question is whether this righteousness and holiness was natural to the first man or not. To answer it, the teachers of the Roman Church point out that "natural" is used in several ways.

First, whatever one has from birth is called natural, and in this sense natural is opposed to acquired. Second, what suits nature, what does not destroy nature but rather adorns and perfects it, is called natural; in this sense natural is opposed to what is against nature.

Third, what is either a part of nature, or flows from nature's principles, or is fitted to flow from them, is called natural. In this sense the body and the soul, the powers of sense and of understanding, and the acts those powers perform without help that goes beyond nature, are called natural, and so natural is opposed to supernatural.

source_text: IV. Jam vero nonnulli sunt inter Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, qui justitiam & sanctitatem illam, quae, fatente tota Ecclesia Romana, in primis parentibus ante peccatum reperiebatur, pertendant naturalem modis omnibus fuisse, & non solum quatenus naturale distinguitur ab adventitio, sive ab eo quod est contra naturam; sed etiam quatenus opponitur supernaturali. Nec enim justitiam illam fuisse gratiam supernaturalem, sed ad naturalem hominis nondum corrupti statum pertinuisse, & fuisse conditionem naturae integrae debitam. Id testatur Medina in 1. 2. quaest. 18. articulo 2. Intelligunt, inquit, Doctores quidam per hominem constitutum in puris naturalibus hominem constitutum in natura integra, cum dono & vigore sanante naturam, adeo ut in bono & officio virtutum posset permanere, & perseverare si vellet; Quae sententia sine dubio videtur esse Augustini. Et hi sunt viri illi insigniter eruditi, qui, teste Bellarmino, censent idem sensisse Thomam ipsum cum caeteris authoribus probatioribus, & eos hac in parte contrarium tenuisse ejus quod Bellarminus ipse docet.
english: Some teachers of the Roman Church, however, maintain that the righteousness and holiness which the whole Roman Church agrees was found in our first parents before sin was natural in every sense. It was natural, they say, not only as natural is distinguished from acquired or from what is against nature, but also as it is opposed to supernatural. That righteousness was not supernatural grace; it belonged to the natural state of man not yet corrupted, and was a condition owed to unfallen nature.

Medina bears witness to this on the Prima Secundae, question 18, article 2: "Some teachers understand by 'man placed in a purely natural state' man placed in unfallen nature, with a gift and strength that heals nature, so that he could remain in the good and in the practice of the virtues and persevere if he chose. This opinion is without doubt Augustine's."

These are the remarkably learned men who, as Bellarmine reports, think that Thomas himself held the same view along with the other more reputable authors, and that on this point they held the opposite of what Bellarmine himself teaches.

source_text: V. Verum haec sententia fuit a Pontificibus Romanis videlicet, Pio V. & Gregorio XIII. superiori saeculo damnata. Nam inter multos articulos in singulari Bulla horum Pontificum damnatos, iste est vigesimus primus. Humanae naturae sublimatio, & exaltatio in consortium divinae debita fuit integritati primae conditionis, ac proinde naturalis dicenda est, non supernaturalis. Sextus vero & vigesimus his verbis conceptus est, Integritas primae conditionis non fuit indebita humanae naturae exaltatio, sed ejus naturalis conditio. Ut refert Bellarminus de gratia primi hominis, lib. unico, cap. 1.
english: Popes Pius V and Gregory XIII condemned this view in the last century. In their bull, which condemned many articles together, it appears as article 21: "Human nature's being lifted up and raised into partnership with the divine nature was owed to the integrity of man's first condition, and is therefore to be called natural, not supernatural."

Article 26 runs: "The integrity of man's first condition was not an exaltation of human nature beyond its due, but its natural condition." Bellarmine records this in chapter 1 of his single book On the Grace of the First Man.

source_text: VI. Itaque Doctorum Ecclesiae Romanae communis sententia est, justitiam & sanctitatem, qua primus homo ante lapsum ornatus erat, naturalem quidem dici posse, quatenus naturale opponitur ei quod est contra naturam, & significat id quod est naturae consentaneum, & quod naturam non destruit, sed ornat & perficit: aut etiam quatenus naturale opponitur ei quod est adventitium, & significat id quod inest ab origine, seu a nativitate. Admittunt enim primum nostrum parentem in justitia fuisse creatum: & idcirco justitiam illam, qua in integritatis statu praeditus erat, vocant Originalem. Sed negant istam justitiam fuisse naturalem, quatenus naturale opponitur supernaturali; quia scilicet, ex eorum mente, ex principiis naturae non fluxit, sed fuit donum Dei gratuitum, quod hominem supra naturalem conditionem evexit.
english: The common view of the Roman Church's teachers, then, is that the righteousness and holiness with which the first man was adorned before the fall can indeed be called natural in two senses. It is natural as opposed to what is against nature, meaning what suits nature and does not destroy it but adorns and perfects it. It is natural too as opposed to what is acquired, meaning what is there from the origin, or from birth.

For they grant that our first parent was created in righteousness, and so they call the righteousness he had in his unfallen state original righteousness. But they deny that it was natural as natural is opposed to supernatural, because in their view it did not flow from nature's principles but was God's free gift, which raised man above his natural condition.

source_text: VII. Ut autem hac in parte mentem suam clarius explicent, observant aliquid supernaturale dici duobus modis, per se & per accidens. Per se dicitur supernaturale, quod ex genere suo non est aptum fluere ex principiis naturae: qualis fuit ascensus Eliae igneo curru in coelum, robur Sampsonis, & alia id genus. Per accidens supernaturale vocatur quod interdum obtinetur divino miraculo, licet alioquin ex naturae principiis fluere soleat. Talis fuit sensus videndi quem Dominus caeco nato restituit: sapientia Salomoni divinitus tributa, & alia non pauca quae in scripturis leguntur.
english: To make their meaning clearer on this point, they note that something is called supernatural in two ways, in itself (per se) and by circumstance (per accidens).

What by its very kind is not fitted to flow from nature's principles is supernatural in itself, like Elijah's going up to heaven in a fiery chariot, Samson's strength, and other things of that sort. What is sometimes obtained by a divine miracle, though otherwise it usually flows from nature's principles, is supernatural by circumstance. Such was the sight the Lord gave back to the man born blind, the wisdom God gave Solomon, and many other things we read in Scripture.

source_text: VIII. Jam autem justitiae donum in primo homine volunt supernaturale fuisse, non tantum per accidens, quia nimirum fuerit gratis & immediate, & modo quodam naturam superante a Deo collatum: sed etiam per se, & ex suo genere quia justitia illa quae primum hominem ornabat nec fluxit, nec fluere potuit ex principiis naturae etiam non corruptae. Nec enim posse hominem, etiam nondum peccato infectum, propriis naturae viribus Deum & nosse & amare, quantum requirit justitia & sanctitas Deo grata & accepta, ad vitae & beatitudinis aeternae praemium. Neque etiam per solas vires & dona naturae posse corpus animae, sensumque & appetitum rationi ita perfecte subjici; ut nulla in homine existat carnis adversus spiritum rebellio, neque ullam in bene agendo difficultatem & repugnantiam, aut ad male agendum proclivitatem in se experiatur, sicuti res in homine integro se habebat, in quo scilicet nulli erant inordinati, & adversus rectam rationem rebelles concupiscentiae motus.
english: They hold, then, that the gift of righteousness in the first man was supernatural not only by circumstance, because God gave it freely, directly and in a way beyond nature, but also in itself and by its kind, because the righteousness that adorned the first man neither flowed nor could flow from nature's principles, even uncorrupted nature.

Man, even before sin had infected him, could not by nature's own powers know and love God as fully as a righteousness and holiness that pleases God and is accepted by him requires for the reward of eternal life and blessedness.

Nor could nature's powers and gifts alone subject body to soul, and sense and appetite to reason, so perfectly that there was no rebellion of flesh against spirit in man, and that he felt no difficulty or resistance in doing good and no leaning toward doing evil. Yet that is how things stood in unfallen man, in whom there were no disordered movements of concupiscence rebelling against right reason.

source_text: IX. Haec est doctrina Bellarmini de gratia primi hominis libro unico, cap. 4. Ubi haec est ejus quarta propositio, Rectitudo illa cum qua Adamus creatus fuit, & sine qua post ejus lapsum omnes homines nascuntur, donum supernaturale fuit. Quam propositionem ut explicet, observat primo hominem naturaliter constare ex carne & spiritu, & ideo partim cum bestiis, partim cum Angelis communicare naturam: & quidem ratione carnis & communionis cum bestiis, habere propensionem quandam ad bonum corporale & sensibile, in quod fertur per sensum & appetitum: ratione vero spiritus & communionis cum Angelis, habere propensionem ad bonum spirituale & intelligibile, in quod fertur per intelligentiam & voluntatem. Ex his autem diversis vel contrariis propensionibus existere in uno eodemque homine pugnam quandam & ex ea pugna ingentem bene agendi difficultatem, dum una propensio alteram impedit.
english: This is what Bellarmine teaches in chapter 4 of his single book On the Grace of the First Man. His fourth proposition there reads: "The rectitude with which Adam was created, and without which all men have been born since his fall, was a supernatural gift."

To explain it, he first notes that by nature man is made of flesh and spirit, and so shares a nature partly with the beasts and partly with the angels. Because of the flesh, which he shares with the beasts, he has a leaning toward bodily, sensible good, which he pursues through sense and appetite. Because of the spirit, which he shares with the angels, he has a leaning toward spiritual, intelligible good, which he pursues through understanding and will.
From these different, even opposed, leanings a kind of conflict arises within one and the same man, and from that conflict a great difficulty in doing good, as one leaning hinders the other.

source_text: X. Deinde dicit divinam providentiam initio creationis, ut remedium adhiberet huic morbo seu languori naturae humanae, qui ex conditione materiae oriebatur, addidisse homini donum quoddam insigne, justitiam videlicet Originalem, qua veluti aureo quodam fraeno pars inferior parti superiori, & pars superior Deo facile subjecta contineretur. Sic autem subjectam carnem spiritui, ut non posset ipso invito moveri, neque ei rebellis fieri, nisi ipse fieret rebellis Deo; in potestate tamen spiritus fuisse Deo rebellem fieri, & non fieri. Unde colligit primi hominis justitiam naturalem quidem fuisse, quatenus naturale dicitur id omne quod habetur a nativitate, & quatenus naturale dicitur id quod est naturae consentaneum, sed non fuisse naturalem, quatenus naturale distinguitur a supernaturali, & significat id quod fluit ex principiis naturae.
english: Next he says that at the beginning of creation divine providence, to remedy this sickness or weakness of human nature arising from the condition of matter, gave man a remarkable gift, original righteousness. By it, as by a golden bridle, the lower part was kept easily subject to the higher, and the higher to God.

The flesh was so subject to the spirit that it could not be moved against the spirit's will or rebel against it unless the spirit itself rebelled against God, though it was in the spirit's power to rebel against God or not.

From this he concludes that the first man's righteousness was natural in the sense that whatever one has from birth is natural, and in the sense that what suits nature is natural; but it was not natural in the sense in which natural is distinguished from supernatural and means what flows from nature's principles.

source_text: XI. Adversarii, inquit, censent rectitudinem illam in qua creatus est Adam fuisse illi naturalem hoc ultimo modo (nempe quatenus naturale opponitur supernaturali) nimirum quod fuerit veluti quaedam sanitas debita naturae, aptaque nasci ex ipsa natura bene constituta, id est, non corrupta: & nunc hominibus qui eam rectitudinem amiserunt in Adamo, deesse bonum aliquod naturale, quale deesse pecudi, si caeca, vel claudicans, vel febricitans nasceretur. Et nunc, si alicui homini originalis illa justitia divinitus redderetur, dicerent esse donum supernaturale per accidens, non per se, ut diximus de oculis redditis caeco nato. Nos vero existimamus rectitudinem illam, etiam partis inferioris, fuisse donum supernaturale, & quidem per se, non per accidens, ita ut neque ex principiis naturae fluxerit, neque potuerit fluere. Et quia donum illud supernaturale erat, ut statim probaturi sumus, eo remoto, natura humana sibi relicta pugnam illam experiri coepit partis inferioris cum superiore, quae naturalis futura erat, id est, ex conditione materiae sequutura, nisi Deus justitiae donum homini addidisset. Quare non magis differt status hominis post lapsum Adae, a statu ejusdem in puris naturalibus, quam differt spoliatus a nudo: neque deterior est humana natura, si culpam originalem detrahas, neque magis ignorantia & infirmitate laborat, quam esset & laboraret in puris naturalibus condita. Proinde corruptio naturae non ex alicujus doni naturalis carentia, neque ex alicujus malae qualitatis accessu, sed ex sola doni supernaturalis ob Adae peccatum amissione profluxit. Quam sententiam communem esse Doctorum Scholasticorum veterum & recentiorum, multis postea allatis eorum testimoniis probat.
english: "Our opponents," Bellarmine says, "hold that the rectitude in which Adam was created was natural to him in this last sense, that is, as natural is opposed to supernatural. They hold it was a kind of health owed to nature and fitted to arise from nature itself when well formed, that is, uncorrupted. Men who lost that rectitude in Adam now lack some natural good, they say, as a beast would lack one if it were born blind, lame or feverish. And if original righteousness were now restored by God to some man, they would call it a supernatural gift by circumstance, not in itself, as we said of the eyes given back to the man born blind.

"We, however, hold that this rectitude, even in the lower part, was a supernatural gift, and supernatural in itself, not by circumstance, so that it neither flowed nor could flow from nature's principles. And because that gift was supernatural, as we shall prove shortly, once it was taken away human nature, left to itself, began to feel the conflict of lower part against higher that would have been natural, that is, would have followed from the condition of matter, had God not added the gift of righteousness to man.

"So man's state after Adam's fall differs from his state in a purely natural condition no more than a man stripped differs from a man naked. Take away original guilt, and human nature is no worse, and suffers no more from ignorance and weakness, than it would be and would suffer if it had been made in a purely natural condition. The corruption of nature, then, came not from the lack of some natural gift, nor from the addition of some bad quality, but solely from the loss of the supernatural gift because of Adam's sin."
Bellarmine then proves that this is the common view of the scholastic teachers, old and more recent, by citing many of their testimonies.

source_text: XII. Sed quamvis Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae in eo communiter hodie consentiant quod justitia & sanctitas hominis in integritatis & innocentiae statu fuit donum quoddam supernaturale, & gratia proprie sic dicta ac naturae superaddita: inter eos tamen hic restat sententiarum notabile discrimen. Etenim eorum nonnulli justitiam & sanctitatem primi hominis sic volunt fuisse supernaturalem, & ad gratiam non ad naturam pertinuisse, ut fuerit tamen quodammodo innocenti naturae debita. Ita ut impossibile fuerit primum hominem sine tali gratia a Deo condi & creari: quia scilicet, hoc repugnavisset divinae bonitati, justitiae, & sapientiae. Alioquin enim futurum fuisse, ut Deus crearet hominem vel malum, vel miserum, aut potius utrumque. Nam non potest non malus & non miser non esse qui Deum nec novit, nec amat puro & casto amore, prout creaturam rationalem decet: & in quo corporei sensus & appetitus rationem invitam & renitentem trahunt ad haec inferiora, nec mentis imperiis & dictamini parent, sed adversus eam rebellant atque tumultuantur. Est autem bonitati divinae contrarium, ut condat hominem malum & peccatorem, aut saltem miserum, absque ulla ipsius culpa.
english: Although the teachers of the Roman Church now generally agree that man's righteousness and holiness in the state of integrity and innocence was a supernatural gift, grace in the proper sense, added on top of nature, there is still a notable difference of opinion among them.

Some of them hold that the first man's righteousness and holiness was supernatural and belonged to grace rather than to nature, yet was in some way owed to innocent nature. On their view it was impossible for God to make and create the first man without such grace, since that would have been at odds with God's goodness, justice and wisdom. Otherwise God would have created man either bad or wretched, or rather both.

A creature that neither knows God nor loves him with a pure and chaste love, as befits a rational creature, cannot help being bad and wretched. So too one whose bodily senses and appetite drag an unwilling, resisting reason down to lower things, and who do not obey the mind's commands and direction but rebel and riot against it. And it is contrary to God's goodness to make a man bad and a sinner, or at least wretched, through no fault of his own.

source_text: XIII. Itaque non existimant debitum omne cum gratia pugnare, sed solum illud quod in bonis operibus & meritis fundatur. Proinde quamvis Deus, dum creaturam rationalem condit, debeat, id exigente bonitate, & sapientia ejus, ei dona conferre, & auxilia praebere quae necessaria sunt ad Deum puro & casto amore prosequendum, vitamque justam tranquillam & beatam degendam, dona & auxilia ista nihilominus, ex eorum mente, non ad naturam, sed ad gratiam proprie dictam pertinent: quoniam talia dona & auxilia nullo modo meritis creaturae debentur, & creatura ex se ad ista non sufficit, nisi supra naturam a Deo adjuvetur.
english: So they do not think that every kind of debt is at odds with grace, only a debt founded on good works and merits.

When God makes a rational creature, his goodness and wisdom require that he give it the gifts and supply the help it needs to love God with a pure and chaste love and to live a righteous, peaceful and blessed life. Even so, in their view, those gifts and that help belong not to nature but to grace in the proper sense, because they are in no way owed to the creature's merits, and the creature is not equal to them by itself unless God helps it beyond nature.

source_text: XIV. Haec est doctrina eorum qui Jansenii doctrinam & placita sequuntur, ut videre est in brevi Catechismo quem de gratia ediderunt. Ibi enim capite quarto, postquam asseruerunt primum hominem fuisse creatum in statu sanctitatis & justitiae, cognitionis & amoris divini, Deo simul naturam formante, & gratiam communicante, docent hominem in alio statu creari non potuisse: quoniam Deus nihil facere potest quod ordinatum non sit: jam vero creaturam rationalem inordinatam fore, nisi in statu gratiae crearetur. Id autem ita esse probant ex eo, quod creaturae intellectualis ordo essentialis est, ut ad Deum tendat tanquam ad centrum suum, & originem suam. Illuc autem tendere non potest, nisi per auxilium quod gratia subministrat. Unde sequitur creaturam talem futuram extra proprium ordinem, si nondum peccato corrupta, gratia privaretur.
english: This is the teaching of those who follow the doctrine and positions of Jansenius, as can be seen in the short Catechism on grace they published.

In its fourth chapter, after stating that the first man was created in a state of holiness and righteousness, of knowledge and love of God, with God at once forming his nature and giving him grace, they teach that man could not have been created in any other state. God can make nothing that is not well ordered, and a rational creature would be disordered unless it were created in a state of grace.

They prove this from the claim that an intellectual creature's essential order is to tend toward God as toward its center and its source. It cannot tend there except by the help grace supplies. It follows that such a creature, if deprived of grace before it was corrupted by sin, would be outside its proper order.

source_text: XV. Ista petita sunt ex Jansenio ipso qui in libro posthumo, qui Augustinus inscribitur, prolixe doctrinam eandem ex Augustino colligit, probat, & amplificat. Praecipue vero primo & secundo libro de statu naturae purae, ubi multis argumentis confirmat & ostendit hominem non potuisse in statu naturae purae, sine omni gratia creari: quia per solas naturae, etiam non corruptae vires, absque gratiae naturam adjuvantis auxilio, nequit homo Deum ullo vero amore diligere, & ulla qualicunque Dei contemplatione & fruitione beari. Adeoque si Deus supponeretur hominem in statu naturae purae, sine omni gratia creare, necessario illum crearet & malum & miserum: quod Dei bonitati & sapientiae omnino repugnat. Ac praeterea docet gratiam dilectionis Dei, in qua primus homo creatus est, verissimam retinere rationem gratiae, quamvis Deus eam nullo justitiae debito, sed ex condecentia infirmitatis creaturae, ex lege suae sapientiae, suaeque benignitatis, & sanctitatis, & misericordiae propriaeque rectitudinis, creaturae innocenti largiatur, ne alioquin omnia peccata, & dilectio ejus in inferiora diffluens, in ipsum revolvantur Deum, qui ei dilectionem ex nemine nisi ex Deo principio & fine suo religare praecepit. Quae sunt ipsa Jansenii verba, lib. 1. de statu naturae, cap. 20. cujus titulus est, Quomodo Bona voluntas, in qua condi debet creatura rationalis, esset gratia.
english: These points are taken from Jansenius himself, who in his posthumous book entitled Augustinus gathers this same teaching from Augustine at length, proves it and enlarges on it. He does so especially in the first and second books on the state of pure nature.

There he argues at length that man could not have been created in a state of pure nature without any grace at all. By the powers of nature alone, even uncorrupted nature, without the help of grace assisting nature, man cannot love God with any true love or be made blessed by any kind of contemplation and enjoyment of God. So if God were supposed to create man in a state of pure nature without any grace, he would necessarily create him both bad and wretched, which is wholly at odds with God's goodness and wisdom.

He teaches besides that the grace of love for God in which the first man was created keeps the full and true character of grace. God gives it to the innocent creature not as a debt of justice but because it befits the creature's weakness, and by the law of his own wisdom, kindness, holiness, mercy and rectitude. Otherwise all sins, and the creature's love spilling down into lower things, would be laid at God's own door, since he commanded it to bind its love to no one but God, its source and end.
These are Jansenius' own words, in book 1 On the State of Nature, chapter 20, whose title is "How the good will in which a rational creature must be made was grace."

source_text: XVI. Nam ut ibidem videre est, ex ejus sententia, gratiae etiam propriissime dictae non repugnant debita quaelibet, seu connaturalitates, decentiae, congruentiae & aequitates, quae oriuntur ex aliis capitibus, quam ex jure creaturae. Ideoque quamvis nihil connaturalius fuerit creaturae ad imaginem Dei conditae, quam ut cum Dei notitia & amore crearetur: nihilque congruentius, decentius & aequius respectu Dei fuerit, quam ut rationali creaturae innocenti, quae ad Deum velut finem suum naturalem ordinata est, ea darentur quae ad assequendum finem illum necessaria sunt, idque Deus sibi ipsi, suisque attributis quodammodo deberet: attamen illa Dei cognitio atque dilectio, sine qua Deo frui nulla creatura potest, gratia dici meretur, etiam creaturarum innocentium respectu; tum quia nullis meritis creaturae debetur, tum quia cognitio & dilectio hujusmodi naturae cujuscunque creatae vires superat, nisi supra naturam a Deo adjuvetur.
english: As can be seen in the same place, Jansenius holds that grace, even in the strictest sense, is not contradicted by any kind of debt, whether called connaturality, seemliness, fittingness or equity, so long as it arises from some other source than the creature's own right.

Nothing could be more connatural to a creature made in God's image than to be created with knowledge and love of God. On God's side, nothing could be more fitting, seemly and equitable than that a rational, innocent creature, ordered to God as its natural end, should be given what it needs to reach that end; in a sense God owed this to himself and to his attributes.

Yet that knowledge and love of God, without which no creature can enjoy God, deserves to be called grace even with respect to innocent creatures. It is owed to no merit of the creature, and knowledge and love of that kind surpass the powers of any created nature unless God helps it beyond nature.

source_text: XVII. Sed in diversum abit communior Doctorum Scholae Romanae sententia. Etenim existimant justitiam & sanctitatem, quae in primo homine fuit, non solum fuisse donum supernaturale, & quod ad naturam non ad gratiam pertinebat; sed etiam aliquid naturae humanae, quamvis innocenti & nondum peccatrici, prorsus indebitum: ita ut nihil repugnaret sapientiae, bonitati, & justitiae divinae hominem sine tali justitia creari. Unde est quod inter status hominis possibiles ponunt statum purae naturae, sive hominis, ut loquuntur, in puris naturalibus. In quo statu ex eorum mente, homo nec justus, nec injustus esset: nec ullius peccati reus nec etiam ulla gratia praeditus.
english: The more common view among the teachers of the Roman school goes another way. They hold that the righteousness and holiness of the first man was not only a supernatural gift, belonging to grace and not to nature, but also something wholly unowed to human nature, even innocent nature not yet sinful. So it would not have been at odds with God's wisdom, goodness and justice for man to be created without such righteousness.

That is why they count among man's possible states the state of pure nature, or, as they put it, of man in a purely natural condition. In that state, as they see it, man would be neither righteous nor unrighteous, neither guilty of any sin nor endowed with any grace.

source_text: XVIII. Nam ut mentem Scholasticorum hac in parte refert & explicat jam dictus Jansenius, de statu naturae purae libro primo capite primo, juxta illos, pura natura dicitur puritate negativa, quia scilicet, nihil habet superadditum sive bonum, sive malum, quod ei debitum non sit: ita neque peccatum habeat, poenamque peccati comitem, neque ullum gratiae naturam superantis donum.
english: Jansenius, already mentioned, reports and explains the scholastics' view on this in book 1, chapter 1 of On the State of Pure Nature. On their account nature is called pure by a negative purity: nothing is added to it, good or bad, beyond what is owed to it. It has neither sin, nor the punishment that goes with sin, nor any gift of grace beyond nature.

source_text: XIX. Ut vero facile intelligatur, quid hujusmodi naturae status comprehendat, naturam lapsam intueri jubent, in qua quicquid praeter peccati reatum deprehendimus, hoc ad puram naturam pertinere profitentur. Quippe Regula solennis eorum est, naturam puram a natura lapsa discrepare sicut nudum a spoliato, qui non aliter differunt, nisi quod hic amiserit, quod alter nunquam habuit: ut proinde pura natura se habeat instar negationis, lapsa instar privationis.
english: To make it easy to see what such a state of nature includes, they tell us to look at fallen nature: whatever we find in it apart from the guilt of sin, they say, belongs to pure nature.

Their set rule is that pure nature differs from fallen nature as the naked man differs from the man stripped. The two differ only in that the one has lost what the other never had. So pure nature is like a negation, fallen nature like a privation.

source_text: XX. Itaque quum docent hominem a Deo creari posse, nullo omnino praecedente peccato, in statu naturae purae, id sibi volunt hominem eo casu creandum esse sine ordinatione ad beatitudinem sempiternam, seu claram visionem Dei, & consequenter sine fide in intellectu, & sine charitate Deum diligente condendum. Praeterea repugnantiam illam carnis & spiritus, quam in nobis experimur, tali homini fore prorsus naturalem. Usque adeo ut ordo mere naturalis postulet, ut Deus duos illos appetitus contrarios reciprocis motibus conflictari sinat, neque concursum suum subtrahendo, neque dono quopiam superaddito mutuam pugnam hostilitatemque comprimendo.
english: So when they teach that God could create man in a state of pure nature with no prior sin at all, they mean that man would then be created without any ordering to eternal blessedness, that is, to the clear vision of God, and so would be made without faith in his intellect and without charity loving God.

They mean too that the conflict of flesh and spirit we experience would be wholly natural to such a man. The merely natural order would even require God to let those two opposed appetites clash back and forth, neither withdrawing his concurrence nor checking their mutual conflict and hostility by any added gift.

source_text: XXI. Ac proinde quantum ad internas animi vires, tantam in pura natura futuram ignorantiam, beneque cogitandi, judicandi, & vivendi infirmitatem, peccandique pronitatem, quantam in natura lapsa experimur. Quantum ad externa vero majorem. Nam praeterquam quod objecta sensibilia concupiscentiam excitantia essent eadem, mala pravorum hominum consilia, & exempla potentius tunc ad malum provocarent. Nam cognitio Dei virtutumque quae Adamo communicata fuerat, & memoria promissionum & comminationum Dei, priorisque status & praeteriti lapsus recordatio, & promissio venturi Christi, cum spe redemptionis ejus, quae per traditionem a capite in posteros diffusa promanarunt; peccandi facilitatem in natura lapsa mitigare potuerunt, ut hac in parte caecitas, corruptio morum generalior, peccandique pronitas in pura natura proclivior futura fuisse videatur.
english: So with regard to the inner powers of the soul, there would be as much ignorance in pure nature, as much weakness in thinking, judging and living well, and as much proneness to sin, as we experience in fallen nature. With regard to outward things there would be more.

The sense objects that stir up desire would be the same, and besides that, the evil counsel and example of wicked men would then urge men to evil more strongly. For in fallen nature the ease of sinning could be softened by what had come down by tradition from the head of the race to his descendants: the knowledge of God and of the virtues that had been given to Adam, the memory of God's promises and threats, the recollection of the former state and of the fall, and the promise of the coming Christ with the hope of his redemption.
So on this score blindness, a more widespread corruption of morals, and the tendency to sin would apparently have been greater in pure nature.
